div.p: One of the core functions of an operating system is scheduling applications such that overall system provides a satisfactory result. Real-time embedded systems have an additional requisite to provide correct output within deadline; failure could be catastrophic for safety critical systems. In this paper, the feasibility of Primary-Backup Fault Tolerant Scheduling (PB-FTS) to handle application level faults by means of switching between primary and secondary copy of task is examined. PB-FTS, which is the secondary scheduler, is evaluated over the different traditional scheduling algorithms such as Rate Monotonic (RM), Deadline Monotonic (DM) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) under various fault scenarios. The fault handling capacity and performance of PB-FTS is measured by running MATLAB based simulations. Simulation results indicate a decreasing trend in fault handling capacity from 100% at 0.6 utilization factor for one fault to 53% at 1.0 utilization factor for three faults.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Ever increasing use of digital systems in daily life has made us so comfortable and ease that our life runs around digital solutions. These solutions basically flow from two types of systems: non-real time and real time systems. They may also be classified as: non-safety critical systems and safety critical systems. There are many examples for each combination of classification and the focus here is on real time safety critical systems. A classical example would be a satellite launch vehicle and other aerospace applications [1] [2]. Nuclear power plant, air traffic control or an insulin pump are other instances of such systems. They require being accurate in their output and time at which the output is produced.

The resource constrained nature of such systems narrows possible designs to make the system fault tolerant. Nevertheless a fault tolerant system can be designed by creating application level redundancy, which delivers an acceptable output within given time limit using Fault Tolerant Scheduling (FTS) despite fault occurrence.

The popular scheduling algorithms for such real-time domain applications are RM, DM and EDF, wherein the application is just a process to be executed before its deadline. The scheduler has no scope of control over the application's success or failure. The idea of FTS is to use fault as a parameter for scheduling tasks, making FTS the secondary scheduler. The aim is to use time or processor redundancy (as per availability) to ensure that, despite failure of an application, an acceptable output is provided by the system [3].
Throughout this paper the following assumptions are considered:

1. There is an Operating System (OS) or Real Time OS (RTOS) present in the system 2. Hardware failure of processor is not part of the scope 3. The terms -process, task and jobs -represent a "developer written program" that is part of the application of the system 4. For every task scheduled, there exist two copies of ita primary copy and a backup copy 5. The backup copy executes faster than the primary copy and provides an acceptable output.

div.head: II. FAULT TOLERANCE AND FAULT TOLERANT SCHEDULING
div.p: Failure, error and fault can be understood in different sense based on the perspective of observer. A failure can be defined as system's incapability to produce output or to provide an acceptable output within given time limit. An error can be defined as the system or a part of system producing an incorrect output, for reasons known or unknown. A fault is defined as a defect in hardware or process or data definition [4]. The events occur in the order: a fault occurs in system, which leads to an error, causing a failure. Fault Tolerance is understood as the capability of system to provide an acceptable output in presence of fault [4].

There are three types of faults: (a) permanent fault, (b) transient fault and (c) intermittent fault. These faults can occur at different levels/parts of the system, which are: hardware, OS and application. Thus, there are four types of fault tolerance: (a) hardware fault tolerance, (b) software fault tolerance, (c) temporal fault tolerance and (d) information fault tolerance [5].

There are various methods to handle faults, based on type and level at which the fault is addressed, such as hot-standby method in hardware fault tolerance. One can also design a cross-level technique such as software based hardware fault tolerance [5]. All techniques involve creation of redundancies in some form or other. By same logic, to address application faults at kernel level, we need application redundancy. Application redundancy helps in handling application faults but it is feasible only if an OS can perform swapping between copies of application. This operation is performed by secondary scheduler when a failure occurs during run-time.

There are many fault tolerant scheduling algorithms available such as: (a) N-version programming, (b) Primary Backup, (c) Imprecise Computational model, (d) (M, K) deadline model etc [5]. Basic idea and working principle of using primary backup approach on different versions of multiprocessor systems is presented in [6].

In [7] a primary-backup based fault-tolerant and RRFTGS (Resource Reclaim Fault Tolerant Global Scheduling) is proposed. This scheduling proved mathematically to be more efficient than Global Scheduling (GS) and Fault Tolerant Global Scheduling (FTGS-1). In [8], authors have compared 3 approaches of Primary-Backup for fault tolerant scheduling: (a) Primary-backup exclusive, (b) Primary-backup concurrent, and (c) Primary-backup overlapping, using object-based task model for simulation. This paper focuses on examining system schedulability when PB-FTS is used with RM, DM and EDF scheduling algorithms under various fault occurrences for a single processor system. The end goal is to find an optimal utilization factor for a higher probability of fault handling under PB-FTS.

div.head: III. METHODOLOGY
div.p: The methodology used in this paper is step simulation. The goal is to observe whether the system is schedulable or not, when each task successfully meets its deadline, despite occurrence of fault. Schedulability of the system is checked using two different approaches: (a) Mathematical analysis and (b) Deadline miss during simulation.

Mathematical analysis is performed to check inherent schedulability of system for a particular scheduling algorithm. The scheduling algorithms under study are RM, DM and EDF. div.head: IV. SYSTEM MODELING
div.p: The model to exhibit the behavior of system is generated using MATLAB. The model consists of 5 tasks to test output against each defined system parameter (table 1). These parameters are co-dependent; changing value of causes changes in and changing value of causes change in hyperperiod. There are many combinations in which a system can be defined based on these parameters. To create consistency and linearity in results, a fixed time period for all tasks such that the hyper-period is fixed at 60 is considered. is an indicator of CPU loading, which is derived when a system is designed. To observe the behaviour of PB-FTS, the system is tested with utilization factors ranging from 0.6 to 1 at an increment of 0.1. Keeping constant, there are many possible combinations of system parameters which result in same U. Such combination is called a test case (TC). There is 1 test case for RM and 3 test cases for DM and EDF.

div.head: A. Fault Model
div.p: The application failure detection for the scheduler occurs at every tick as system has single processor. This detection is indicated by the fault model. In the simulation environment, the fault model generates a signal of fault detection and is used by PB-FTS to activate the backup application after suspending the primary. Such a single run simulation is termed as scenario. In order to examine PB-FTS, multiple scenarios are generated and its schedulability is checked.

div.head: 1) One Fault model:
div.p: A fault occurs during the hyperperiod, which can occur at any tick from 1 to 60, meaning there are 60 possible scenarios of fault. 2) Two fault model: Two faults occur within the hyperperiod, between any ticks from 1 to 60. If first fault occurs at tick 1, then there are 59 other possible ticks for second fault (tick 2 to 60). Likewise if the first fault occurs at tick 15, then there are 45 possible ticks for second fault (tick 16 to 60) and so on. Hence, there are 1770 fault scenarios.
3) Three fault model: In this model, occurrence of three faults within hyper-period is simulated. As explained in 2 faults model above, the faults occurrence pattern will generate 34220 scenarios.

div.head: V. SIMULATION
div.p: The pattern of application execution is repeated after hyperperiod time, logically that means the system behaviour will be similar over every hyper-period including for the faults. Therefore, one can predict the system behaviour with fault in a hyper-period; by the pattern, since it is expected to repeat over all hyper-period lengths. Hence, the system is to be simulated for hyper-period length.

The block diagram in Fig. 1 provides an overview of simulation. The first step is analysing mathematically the system for the particular test case for successful schedulability. Next, the system is simulated for every tick. The fault model provides information regarding the occurrence of faultnumber of fault occurred and the tick at which fault is detected. Upon detection of fault, the PB-FTS suspends the primary copy of the task and activates the backup for execution. At each tick, all tasks are checked for a deadline miss.

Output: 1(one) for successful fault handling, no deadline miss. 0(zero) for unsuccessful fault handling, deadline miss occurs. 9 shows the simulation results for 1 fault in hyperperiod length, for which we observed that for RM, PB-FTS can guarantee fault handling for ≤ 0.8 where as for = 0.9 there is 85% probability that fault would be handled. For DM, PB-FTS guarantees fault handling at ≤ 0.7 where as for = 0.8 there is a 98% probability that fault would be handled; and EDF provides a probability of 98% for = 1 and guaranteeing fault handling for ≤ 0.9. For different test cases, as the deadline is more stringent than the earlier case, we do observe a decrease in probability of fault handling.

Table 10 shows the simulation results for 2 faults in hyperperiod length, for which we observed that for RM, PB-FTS can guarantee fault handling for ≤ 0.7 where as for = 0.8 -99% probability and = 0.9 -74% probability that fault would be handled. For DM, PB-FTS guarantees fault handling at ≤ 0.6 where as for = 0.6 and = 0.7 there is a 99% and 94%, respectively, probability that fault would be handled; and EDF provides a probability of 94% & 98% for = 1 and = 0.9 respectively, while guaranteeing fault handling for ≤ 0.8.

Table 11 shows the simulation results for 3 faults in hyperperiod length, for which we observed that for RM, PB-FTS can guarantee fault handling for ≤ 0.6 where as for = 0.7 -99% probability, = 0.8 -97% probability and = 0.9 -66% probability that fault would be handled. For DM, PB-FTS guarantees fault handling at ≤ 0.6 where as for = 0.7 and = 0.8 there is a 99% and 90%, respectively, probability that fault would be handled; and EDF provides a probability of 90% for = 1, 99% for = 0.9 and guaranteeing fault handling for ≤ 0.8. It is evident that as the deadline decreases, the success ratio also decreases.

The comparative graph for EDF scheduler with PB-FTS for all simulation scenarios are summarized in Fig. 2 and similar graphs can be observed for other scheduling algorithms. In this paper, PB-FTS is evaluated for its fault handling capability with conventional scheduling algorithms viz., RM, DM and EDF. Various simulation scenarios were considered with varied utilization factor and fault occurrences. The obtained results indicate that PB-FTS is capable of handling application faults optimally at utilization factor of 0.7 indicated by the higher success ratio; although all possible test scenarios are yet to be considered such as more than five tasks and different scheduling algorithms. Further PB-FTS could be evaluated for other scheduling algorithms and there is also scope to implement PB-FTS as a part of a RTOS or through a framework [12].
